title: Your sunset
tomorrow: every night Seneca put himself on trial. what were the charges?

lines: A HYMN AT THE LIGHTING OF THE LAMPS.
cards: Phones go up on every balcony when the sky turns orange. Early Christians did something with that hour too.
Basil of Caesarea, a bishop, wrote that the fathers thought it right not to receive the gift of the evening light in silence, but to give thanks the moment it appeared.
And he mentions an old hymn the people sang at the lighting of the lamps, a hymn so old he couldn't say who had written it.

teach.b: Today's question: why mark the sunset at all?
The Christian answer lives in that lamp-lighting hymn, known by its Greek name, Phos Hilaron, joyful light.
It greets Christ as the joyful light of the Father's glory, and, coming to the setting of the sun and seeing the evening light, praises Father, Son and Holy Spirit.

It is still sung at Vespers, the evening prayer, in Orthodox churches. That's the teaching: in Christian evening prayer, sunset isn't only the day ending. The lamp you light becomes thanks for a light that stays.
Now a neighbor, in its own terms.
In Islam the day's prayers follow the sun's path, and one of them, maghrib, is prayed just after sunset. The Qur'an asks for prayer at the two ends of the day and in some watches of the night.
What's shared: neither tradition lets the light go without turning to God, right at the hinge of the day.

An honest difference: the Phos Hilaron is a hymn sung to Christ as the light itself, within the Christian faith in the Trinity; maghrib is a set prayer to God, facing Mecca, with bowing and prostration, prayed in the same form every evening.
Two ways of meeting dusk, each in its own house, neither standing in for the other.
On your own path, sunset can become a small rite of yours, with its sources named: one light switched on, one breath of thanks, the day turning.

how: Orthodox Vespers sings the Phos Hilaron, the old lamp-lighting hymn, and maghrib, one of the Muslim daily prayers, is prayed just after sunset; on this path a dusk rite is borrowed with its source named.

o: a small rite of thanks as the daylight goes
the time you stop working and switch on the TV
an evening workout before the light is gone

games.q: the hinge of the day: tap the pairs.
p: the hymn at the lighting of the lamps
evening light not received in silence

s: early Christians let the evening pass without a word
Basil says the fathers chose to give thanks the moment the evening light appeared.
Basil couldn't say who wrote the lamp-lighting hymn
he calls it an ancient form that the people sang.
the Phos Hilaron and maghrib are one prayer in two languages
both turn to God at dusk; one is a hymn to Christ as light, the other a set prayer facing Mecca.

games.q: two coworkers: one steps out just after sunset to pray maghrib, the other lights a lamp at dusk and hums an old hymn. what's an honest way to say what they share?
o: both turn to God as the light goes, each in their own prayer.
it's one ritual with two names, so which one doesn't matter.
only one of them is really praying; the other is just being cozy.
games.why: the hinge of the day is shared; the prayers are not the same. each keeps its own words, its own God-language, its own form.

practice: Look at one source of light near you: a window going gold, a lamp, a candle. Watch it for a few breaths and give it a quiet thank you, the way the old hymn greeted the lamp. Then close your eyes and keep the glow in mind.

wordCard.voice: Your sunset: a small rite at the hinge of the day. In the Phos Hilaron, thanks as the lamps are lit; in Islam, maghrib just after the sun goes down.

orig.note: Greek: joyful light, the old Christian hymn for the lighting of the lamps.

carryVoice: Here's the line for dusk: the day turns, and you turn toward the light. Good evening.
